definition: Linchpin means something that holds the separate parts of a whole together.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word linchpin. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know linchpin should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The night-shift dispatcher turned out to be the linchpin of the depot; the week she retired, three departments discovered none of them actually talked to each other.
Contributor stops short of linchpin — a contributor helps the machine run; losing one slows it, not stops it.
Mainstay stops short of linchpin — a mainstay carries much of the load, but a linchpin is the piece whose loss makes the whole thing fall apart.

A cornerstone is the foundation stone a building rises from — the thing everything else was built on and grew out of. A linchpin holds the finished parts together right now: pull it out and the working whole falls apart. A building's origins point back to its cornerstone; a working system holds together at its linchpin.

A keystone is the wedge at the crown of an arch — pull it and the arch falls — so the word carries grandeur and scale. A linchpin does the same holding work in humbler form: the small pin nobody notices until the wheel comes off. Keystone suits an imposing essential; linchpin, one that looks small.

Linch- is a fossil: Old English lynis named the axle itself, and outside this one compound the word died out centuries ago. Pin, its other half, is everyday English but carries no hidden meaning to unlock. So the word has no family to spot — only the picture of the little pin that keeps the wheel on.
Linchpin means something that holds the separate parts of a whole together.

On paper the aunts' cookie exchange was casual, but Aunt Bea was its linchpin — she kept the address list, brokered peace over the disputed shortbread recipe, and booked the church hall; the winter she stayed in Arizona, the whole tradition simply failed to happen.

Linchpin is more exact than 'important part' because it names the piece whose removal makes the rest fall apart — on a cart, the literal linchpin is the small pin that keeps the wheel on its axle: lose it, and everything stops.
Linchpin praises by warning — it says this piece matters because everything fails without it.

Keystone, which you'll meet in this unit's reference list, draws the same picture from architecture, the wedge at an arch's crown; linchpin is the humbler cart-shop version, best when the essential piece looks small: a scheduler, a translator, a night dispatcher.

The sorting hub on Delmar Street looks unremarkable: a rented garage, two conveyor belts, and a corkboard of route maps.
Yet the whole county's recycling program routes through it.
Collection trucks cannot legally store material overnight, so everything they gather must be weighed, sorted, and released the same day.
When a burst pipe closed the garage for nine days last March, the effects surprised even the planners.
Curbside pickup halted in eleven towns, two mills downstream ran short of baled paper, and the county paid landfill fees it had not budgeted.
A consultant's report later called the hub the linchpin of the entire operation, noting that no other site was licensed to do its work.
The county now keeps a second garage on standby -- an admission of how much had quietly depended on one building.
